evidence_quotes.quote: Against this background, this study investigates the sustainability of urban water and sanitation services in Beira, Mozambique.

Respondents consistently emphasised the problem of fragmented and overlapping mandates among AIAS, AdRC, SASB, and the Municipality. While national legislation assigns responsibilities, operational boundaries remain unclear, often leading to duplication or inaction.
Institutional actors explained that tariffs remain too low to ensure cost recovery, forcing reliance on cross-subsidies and donor financing.
Water committees in Chipangara and Macuti operated with minimal resources and lacked legal recognition, limiting their effectiveness.

The research was conducted in Beira, Sofala Province, Mozambique. Fieldwork took place between 10 June and 25 July 2025 and involved interviews with institutional representatives and community leaders from the neighbourhoods of Ponta Gêa, Chipangara, and Macuti.

In contrast, Chipangara faces systemic failures: entire units have experienced more than a year without piped water, despite continuing to receive water bills. The infrastructure is old and frequently damaged, and responses to breakdowns are often delayed or absent.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community urban water supply (piped network connections and neighbourhood standpipes) and sanitation service access and delivery in three neighbourhoods of Beira, Mozambique.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines legal, institutional, regulatory, and governance factors shaping urban WASH delivery in Beira (Water Law, National Water Policy, draft Water and Sanitation Law, inter-agency governance, and community participation). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, although framed within a five-dimensional sustainability assessment, the study directly empirically examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access and continuity: (1) utility ownership/delegated management and regulatory/statutory mandate allocation across AdRC (operating under delegated management from FIPAG), AIAS, SASB, CRA, and the Beira Municipal Council directly governing repair responsibility and complaint resolution; (2) formal/legal recognition of community water committees governing self-managed standpipes and user-fee reinvestment (formally recognised by FIPAG in Ponta Gêa vs. lacking legal recognition in Chipangara and Macuti); and (3) tariff and cost-recovery rules, including social tariffs that do not cover operational costs, weak payment enforcement, and billing households without piped water delivery.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative empirical socio-legal/governance case study combining a sectoral policy review with primary semi-structured in-person interviews (n = 6: 3 institutional representatives and 3 community leaders) conducted in June–July 2025, analysed via hybrid deductive-inductive thematic coding with verified inter-coder reliability (Cohen's Kappa = 0.81). Qualitative socio-legal studies with identifiable primary data and methods are eligible for the systematic review.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative empirical outcomes directly relevant to service availability, connection coverage, continuity/reliability, repair responsiveness, exclusion, and affordability across three neighbourhoods (e.g., over a year without piped water in parts of Chipangara while still receiving bills, week-long outage following pipe bursts forcing reliance on wells and informal vendors, latrine/sewage overflows, and standpipe service stability in Ponta Gêa).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (City of Beira focusing on Ponta Gêa, Chipangara, and Macuti neighbourhoods; 6 purposively/snowball-sampled institutional and community interviewees), rule-type institutional/regulatory and tariff exposures, qualitative service access/continuity/affordability outcomes, and qualitative phenomenological study design are all clearly identified.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (field interviews conducted in Portuguese with Sena translation assistance).

study_design: Qualitative phenomenological case study combining critical policy review with in-person semi-structured interviews (hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis)
population_and_sample: Urban WASH sector in the City of Beira, Sofala Province, Mozambique, focusing on three neighbourhoods (Ponta Gêa, Chipangara, and Macuti); n = 6 semi-structured interview participants comprising 3 institutional representatives (SASB, AdRC, AIAS) and 3 neighbourhood community leaders
exposure: Mozambique's normative, regulatory, and institutional WASH governance framework in Beira, specifically statutory/operational mandate allocation across utilities and agencies (AdRC under FIPAG delegated management, AIAS, SASB, CRA, and Beira Municipal Council), formal/legal recognition of community standpipe committees, and tariff/cost-recovery rules (social tariffs, billing practices, and payment enforcement)
outcome: Household and neighbourhood water and sanitation service availability, continuity/reliability (frequency and duration of piped supply disruptions, repair responsiveness, reliance on informal vendors and wells), standpipe operation, and perceived affordability across neighbourhoods
rationale: This qualitative phenomenological study (policy review plus 6 semi-structured interviews with utility/agency officials and neighbourhood leaders in Beira, Mozambique) satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings. Beyond general climate and maintenance themes, it empirically investigates rule-type institutional, regulatory, and tariff mechanisms directly governing household and standpipe service access and continuity: overlapping statutory/operational mandates across delegated utility AdRC (under FIPAG), AIAS, SASB, CRA, and the Municipality that stall breakdown repairs and complaint handling; formal/legal recognition of community committees managing standpipes and user fees (recognised by FIPAG in Ponta Gêa vs. unrecognised in Chipangara and Macuti); and tariff/cost-recovery rules (social tariffs below operational cost, weak payment enforcement, and continued billing during year-long piped water outages). Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis.
